note: The side door "Holy shit, the sky is falling": one evening and one store run, sized for three days at home. It is not a section and is counted nowhere. Each line points at the action or actions that own its job: `ids` are the actions the line's tick box stands for (the line is ticked when all of them are, and ticking it ticks them); `also` are actions it links to for a condition some homes do not have, which its tick leaves alone. A line with no `ids` has no box. `only` hides a line for a household whose setup says it does not apply (otherwise a line is hidden when none of its actions apply); with no setup every line shows, and `cold` is its wording then, with the condition in words. `buy` names products: the page links each one's Standard pick, or its only pick, with its price, and prints no tier names. `dont` lines have no boxes; `from` is the action whose rule and sources a line takes, and `own` marks this site's own advice.
title: Holy shit, the sky is falling
door: Saw something frightening online? One evening and one store run, sized for three days at home.
open: You saw something frightening. This site cannot tell you whether it is true. It can tell you where a real warning would come from, and what is worth doing tonight either way.

lines.text: Look where a real warning would come from: your power company's outage page, your city or county alerts, the National Weather Service. Not the post.
Turn on emergency alerts on every phone and sign up for your city's.
Charge every phone, power bank and laptop.
Fill every clean bottle, pitcher and pot you have with tap water. This covers you until you get to the store.
Put a flashlight and shoes beside every bed.
Count your medications. Refill anything with under a week left. If one needs a fridge or a machine needs power, ask your doctor or pharmacist tomorrow what to do in an outage.
Pick one out-of-area contact, text them, and write the family's numbers on paper.
Put water bottles in the freezer. If the power goes out, keep the fridge and freezer shut: a closed fridge keeps food safe for up to 4 hours, a full freezer for about 2 days.
If you park in a garage, find out how the car gets out with no power.
Battery lanterns or headlamps, and spare batteries.
A power bank for each phone.
Bottled water: 3 gallons for each person. Two 24-packs covers two adults. What you filled last night is a bonus.
lines.set: Bottled water: 3 gallons for each person. {packs} for your household of {people}. What you filled last night is a bonus.

water.note: Three gallons is the site's 1 gallon a person a day for three days. A 24-pack of 16.9-ounce bottles is 405.6 ounces, about 3.2 gallons.

lines.text: Three days of food you already eat that needs no cooking and no refrigeration, and a manual can opener.
A battery radio.
A carbon monoxide alarm with battery backup, if anything in your home burns gas.
Fill the gas tank.
lines.cold: If you have a car: fill the gas tank.

lines.text: Take out some cash in small bills.
If you have a baby: formula and diapers for three days.
If you have a pet: food and litter for three days.
If you live above the ground floor: a box of heavy trash bags, in case the toilet stops refilling.
Buy a generator for an apartment, or run one indoors or in a garage, ever.
lines.reason: Generator exhaust contains carbon monoxide, a gas you cannot see or smell.

lines.text: Heat your home with an oven, or cook indoors on a grill or camp stove.
lines.reason: Anything that burns fuel gives off carbon monoxide, which builds up unseen in a closed room.

lines.text: Light the place with candles.
lines.reason: Candles start thousands of home fires every year.

lines.text: Store gasoline in your home.
lines.reason: The U.S. Fire Administration says to store gasoline in a shed away from your home.

lines.text: Buy six months of freeze-dried food tonight, or empty your bank account.
Repost it.

close.title: Then stop
close.text: You're set for three days at home. The rest can wait until you've slept.
